title: WIP Schedule & Over/Under Billings (CMA P1-D · feeds FAR/BAR)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the schedule behind $14 million

Real balances: MBG carries $14,480,000.00 in the 14xxxxx WIP account series, and Riverton carries $11,360,000.00. Those balances belong to different entities and must never be combined. They are not cash, billings, or current-period expense. They are accumulated job costs recorded as a balance-sheet asset while the related projects remain in process. A WIP schedule must explain which jobs comprise the total, how much performance has been earned, what has been billed, and whether each estimate is still credible.

The danger is not merely arithmetic. A late vendor invoice understates cost to date. An optimistic estimate to complete overstates percentage complete and gross profit. A reversal posted to the wrong job can manufacture a margin swing. A project can appear profitable while consuming cash because earned revenue exceeds billings. The WIP schedule joins the job-cost system, contract data, billing records, and the GL so those contradictions become visible.

Concept — five columns that drive the answer

For a performance obligation satisfied over time, ASC 606 permits an input method when that method faithfully depicts performance. In construction, cost-to-cost is common:

Percentage complete = eligible costs incurred to date ÷ current estimated total eligible cost

Revenue recognized to date = transaction price × percentage complete

Gross profit recognized to date = revenue recognized to date − cost recognized to date

Contract position = revenue recognized to date − billings to date

A positive contract position means earned revenue exceeds billings: an underbilling presented as a contract asset, subject to the specific contract facts. A negative position means billings exceed earned revenue: an overbilling presented as a contract liability. Billings are not revenue by themselves. Cash collections are not revenue by themselves. Performance drives recognition; billing and collection drive receivables and cash.

The denominator is a forecast, not a historical fact. Estimated total cost equals cost to date plus the latest estimate to complete. It must incorporate approved scope, remaining quantities, committed subcontracts, labor productivity, procurement risk, and known rework. Costs that do not depict performance—such as certain significant uninstalled materials or abnormal waste—may require adjustment rather than mechanically accelerating progress.

Required schedule fields

  • Entity, job, project manager, and cutoff date.
  • Original contract plus approved modifications forming the current transaction price.
  • Original and current estimated total cost.
  • Cost to date, estimate to complete, and percentage complete.
  • Revenue and gross profit recognized to date and in the current period.
  • Billings to date and the resulting contract asset or liability.
  • Prior-period margin and current margin to expose fade or gain.
  • Reconciliation from the job schedule to exact WIP GL balances.

Worked example — a 75% job

Use the following illustrative amounts; the structure is real, but these amounts are not asserted to be an MBG job:

LineCalculationAmount
Contract priceGiven$2,000,000
Estimated total costGiven$1,600,000
Estimated total gross profit$2,000,000 − $1,600,000$400,000
Cost to dateGiven$1,200,000
Percentage complete$1,200,000 ÷ $1,600,00075%
Revenue to date75% × $2,000,000$1,500,000
Gross profit to date$1,500,000 − $1,200,000$300,000
Billings to dateGiven$1,400,000
Contract asset$1,500,000 − $1,400,000$100,000 underbilled

Three independent checks agree. First, 75% of the $400,000 estimated gross profit is $300,000. Second, revenue of $1,500,000 less cost of $1,200,000 is $300,000. Third, earned revenue of $1,500,000 less billings of $1,400,000 is a $100,000 contract asset. The job has performed more than it has billed, so MBG is financing that timing gap until it submits and collects the next billing.

Assume illustratively that prior-period revenue and gross profit were $1,260,000 and $252,000. Current-period revenue is $240,000 and current-period gross profit is $48,000. A cumulative schedule must subtract prior recognized amounts; recording the entire to-date amount again would double count revenue and profit.

Estimate changes, fade, and loss contracts

Now suppose remaining cost is reassessed and current estimated total cost rises from $1,600,000 to an illustrative $1,800,000, while contract price remains $2,000,000. At $1,200,000 cost to date, revised progress is 66.67%. Revised revenue to date is about $1,333,333 and revised gross profit to date is about $133,333. Compared with the original $300,000 cumulative profit, the estimate change creates a $166,667 cumulative catch-up reduction. It does not rewrite issued prior statements; the current estimate changes the cumulative amount required now.

Gross-profit fade is the decline in estimated margin from one reporting date to the next. Here estimated total profit falls from $400,000 to $200,000 and margin falls from 20% to 10%. Fade can signal missed costs, weak productivity, unapproved change orders, purchasing pressure, or premature prior estimates. Gain is the opposite, but unexpected gains also deserve challenge because they may reflect omitted commitments or cutoff errors.

If the current estimate indicates an overall contract loss, recognize the expected loss in full when required by the applicable loss guidance; do not spread it across the remaining percentage. For example, an illustrative $2,000,000 contract with estimated total cost of $2,080,000 has an $80,000 total expected loss. The fact that the job is only partly complete does not justify reporting only a fraction of the expected loss.

From schedule to entries and proof

A conceptual current-period entry records construction expense and revenue for the period and establishes the net contract position as needed by the entity's system design. Billing entries separately debit accounts receivable and credit billings or the contract-position account. Collection separately debits cash and credits receivables. System account names vary, but the schedule must prevent billing activity from becoming a substitute for earned revenue.

For close, freeze a cutoff and reconcile four directions. Costs to date tie by job to JCS and by exact account to the 14xxxxx GL. Contract price ties to executed contracts and approved modifications. Billings tie to the billing subledger. Prior recognized revenue and profit tie to the prior close. Then perform analytical review: jobs over 100% complete, negative estimates to complete, margins outside expectations, large underbillings, stale costs, completed jobs with WIP, and unexplained post-acquisition reversals all require resolution. The MBG $14,480,000.00 balance is not proven merely because a spreadsheet total happens to match; job composition and cutoff must also be valid.

The JCS warning still applies: “Acct Ending Bal” is not cumulative. Derive true balance from beginning plus year-to-date debits minus year-to-date credits. Exact account matching also matters because substring selection can capture unrelated data. Bank ties beat GL for cash, but WIP proof is anchored to supported job detail and the trial balance.

Worked example — one contract across three reporting years

Cumulative catch-up is where most marks are lost, so work a complete contract with illustrative amounts and no shortcuts. Job M-310 has a fixed transaction price of $6,000,000. Progress is measured cost-to-cost.

Year 1. Cost incurred $1,350,000; estimate to complete $3,150,000.

  • Estimated total cost = $1,350,000 + $3,150,000 = $4,500,000
  • Percentage complete = $1,350,000 ÷ $4,500,000 = 30.00%
  • Cumulative revenue = 30.00% × $6,000,000 = $1,800,000
  • Cumulative gross profit = $1,800,000 − $1,350,000 = $450,000
  • Year 1 revenue = $1,800,000 − $0 = $1,800,000; Year 1 gross profit = $450,000

Year 2. Cumulative cost is now $3,300,000 and the estimate to complete has risen to $2,200,000.

  • Revised estimated total cost = $3,300,000 + $2,200,000 = $5,500,000
  • Percentage complete = $3,300,000 ÷ $5,500,000 = 60.00%
  • Cumulative revenue = 60.00% × $6,000,000 = $3,600,000
  • Cumulative gross profit = $3,600,000 − $3,300,000 = $300,000
  • Year 2 revenue = $3,600,000 − $1,800,000 = $1,800,000
  • Year 2 cost = $3,300,000 − $1,350,000 = $1,950,000
  • Year 2 gross profit = $1,800,000 − $1,950,000 = ($150,000)

Check the same answer a second way: cumulative gross profit of $300,000 less prior cumulative gross profit of $450,000 is negative $150,000. Job M-310 reports a loss in Year 2 even though the contract is still profitable overall. That is the cumulative catch-up mechanism at work. Estimated total gross profit fell from $6,000,000 − $4,500,000 = $1,500,000 to $6,000,000 − $5,500,000 = $500,000. Cumulative profit must now equal 60.00% × $500,000 = $300,000, but $450,000 had already been recognized, so the current period absorbs the entire $150,000 pull-back at once.

Year 3. The job completes at total actual cost of $5,650,000.

  • Cumulative revenue = $6,000,000 (100% complete); cumulative gross profit = $6,000,000 − $5,650,000 = $350,000
  • Year 3 revenue = $6,000,000 − $3,600,000 = $2,400,000
  • Year 3 cost = $5,650,000 − $3,300,000 = $2,350,000
  • Year 3 gross profit = $2,400,000 − $2,350,000 = $50,000

Foot the three years: $450,000 − $150,000 + $50,000 = $350,000, which equals the contract's lifetime gross profit. Any three-year schedule that does not foot to lifetime profit contains an arithmetic or catch-up error.

Trap that loses the mark — recognizing the to-date amount as the current amount

The schedule computes cumulative revenue and profit. Current-period amounts are always cumulative-now minus cumulative-through-prior-period. Reporting the $3,600,000 cumulative Year 2 revenue as Year 2 revenue double counts $1,800,000. Equally, do not restate Year 1: a change in the cost estimate is a change in accounting estimate handled prospectively through the current period's catch-up, not a retrospective correction of issued statements.

Worked example — the loss contract

Take a separate illustrative contract, Job R-220, priced at $6,000,000. At the reporting date cost to date is $3,150,000 and the estimate to complete is $3,150,000.

  • Estimated total cost = $3,150,000 + $3,150,000 = $6,300,000
  • Expected total result = $6,000,000 − $6,300,000 = ($300,000) expected loss
  • Percentage complete = $3,150,000 ÷ $6,300,000 = 50.00%
  • Cumulative revenue = 50.00% × $6,000,000 = $3,000,000

The entire expected loss is recognized now, not 50% of it. So required cumulative gross profit is negative $300,000, which means cumulative cost charged against revenue must be $3,000,000 + $300,000 = $3,300,000. Cost actually incurred is only $3,150,000, so the accrued loss provision is $3,300,000 − $3,150,000 = $150,000, recorded as a liability or as a reduction of the contract asset depending on the entity's presentation policy.

If this contract had reported $450,000 of cumulative gross profit at the prior reporting date, the current-period gross profit charge would be negative $300,000 − $450,000 = ($750,000) — the full swing from prior recognition to the required cumulative position.

Trap that loses the mark — spreading the loss over remaining progress

Recognizing 50% of the $300,000 loss because the job is 50% complete is the classic wrong answer. Losses are recognized in full as soon as they are expected; profits are recognized as performance occurs. The asymmetry is deliberate. A related trap is netting the loss provision against the contract asset without disclosing it, which hides a job the reader most needs to see.

Presentation — contract assets and liabilities are not netted across contracts

Contract position is determined contract by contract and presented gross on the balance sheet. Consider three illustrative MBG jobs at the same cutoff.

JobRevenue recognized to dateBillings to datePosition
M-310$1,500,000$1,400,000$100,000 contract asset (underbilled)
R-220$2,750,000$2,980,000$230,000 contract liability (overbilled)
T-118$940,000$940,000$0

The balance sheet shows a $100,000 contract asset and a $230,000 contract liability. It does not show a single $130,000 net liability. Netting destroys the very information the schedule exists to produce: which jobs are financing the customer and which jobs are being financed by the customer. A group total also cannot cross the MBG and Riverton entity boundary.

Denominator sensitivity — why the estimate to complete is the control point

Percentage complete is a ratio, and a ratio can be moved from either end. Hold Job M-310's Year 2 cost to date at $3,300,000 and vary only the estimate to complete.

Estimate to completeEstimated total costPercentage completeCumulative revenueCumulative gross profit
$1,700,000$5,000,00066.00%$3,960,000$660,000
$2,200,000$5,500,00060.00%$3,600,000$300,000
$2,700,000$6,000,00055.00%$3,300,000$0

A $500,000 movement in an unaudited operational estimate moves reported cumulative gross profit by $360,000 in the first step and $300,000 in the second. Nothing in the general ledger changed. That is why the estimate to complete needs the same evidence discipline as a posted invoice: committed subcontract values, remaining quantities priced at current rates, known rework, procurement exposure, and a documented preparer and reviewer. Comparing the project manager's estimate to complete against remaining commitments in the purchasing system is a stronger control than asking whether the number looks reasonable.

Two adjustments deserve their own review. Significant uninstalled materials delivered to the site but not yet incorporated can inflate the numerator and accelerate progress without accelerating performance; the input measure may need adjustment so that revenue on those materials is limited to their cost. Abnormal waste, rework, and inefficiency similarly add to cost incurred without adding to performance, so mechanically letting them raise percentage complete rewards poor execution with recognized profit.

Trap that loses the mark — treating billings or cash as the progress measure

Under a cost-to-cost input method, the percentage is costs over costs. Billings, collections, physical inspection percentages, and schedule percentages are corroborating evidence, never the numerator. If an exam fact pattern supplies billings to date, that figure belongs only in the contract-position line at the bottom of the schedule.

CPA Crossover — FAR and BAR

FAR tests ASC 606's five-step model, over-time criteria, input methods, contract assets, contract liabilities, and estimate changes. BAR emphasizes analysis: why margin moved, whether forecasts are biased, and how underbilling affects liquidity. An underbilling may increase reported current assets while worsening cash flow; an overbilling may support cash while creating a performance obligation. The labels are not value judgments. They are timing positions that must be understood alongside margin and cash.

Practice and recap

  1. Recompute percentage complete from current eligible costs and current estimated total cost.
  2. Recompute cumulative revenue and profit, then subtract prior recognition for current-period amounts.
  3. Compare earned revenue with billings and classify each job's contract position.
  4. Reconcile schedule costs to exact-account JCS detail and the entity's GL.
  5. Challenge fade, gain, unapproved changes, stale WIP, and reversals.
  6. Document whether every amount is real and sourced or illustrative.

Recap: the WIP schedule converts cost records and forecasts into revenue, profit, and contract position. Cost-to-cost is only as reliable as its numerator, denominator, and cutoff. Keep MBG and Riverton separate, keep billings distinct from earnings, and make every cumulative amount tie forward from the prior close.

flashcards.front: What is the cost-to-cost percentage-complete formula?
flashcards.back: Eligible cost incurred to date divided by current estimated total eligible cost.

flashcards.front: Earned revenue exceeds billings. What is the usual position?
flashcards.back: An underbilling/contract asset, subject to the contract facts.

flashcards.front: Billings exceed earned revenue. What is the usual position?

flashcards.back: A decline in estimated job margin between reporting dates.

flashcards.front: How is current-period revenue derived from a cumulative WIP schedule?
flashcards.back: Required revenue to date minus revenue recognized through the prior period.
No. Performance establishes revenue; billing establishes a receivable and changes contract position.

flashcards.front: What are the MBG and Riverton WIP totals?
How should an expected overall contract loss be treated?
flashcards.back: Recognize the required total expected loss immediately under the applicable loss guidance, not merely by percentage complete.

questions.q: Illustrative cost to date is $900,000 and estimated total cost is $1,500,000. What is progress?
At 60% complete on an illustrative $2,000,000 contract, what is cumulative revenue?
Earned revenue is $1,200,000 and billings are $1,350,000. The job is:
questions.explain: Billings exceed earned revenue by $150,000, producing a contract-liability position.

questions.q: Why can a late vendor invoice overstate profit under cost-to-cost?
choices: It understates cost to date and may distort the estimate
questions.explain: Omitted cost can understate expense and can make the cost-based progress measure and forecast unreliable.

questions.q: Cumulative required revenue is $1,500,000 and prior recognized revenue is $1,260,000. Current revenue is:

choices: Contract position is a timing measure that must be assessed with margin and cash
questions.explain: Over/under billing describes timing, not project quality by itself.

questions.q: Which is the strongest WIP close evidence?
choices: A schedule tied to contracts, billing, prior recognition, job detail, and exact GL accounts
questions.explain: A defensible schedule integrates source evidence and reconciles every major input.
